extracted.intended_audience: AP® English teachers and instructors (AP English Language & Literature teachers and graders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scoring and teaching AP® English free-response essays using the new analytic rubric (Thesis; Evidence and Commentary; Sophistication), including decision rules, common scoring pitfalls, and classroom implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (1 point)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position/interpretation" (object varies by question type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must take a position and go beyond merely restating the prompt or summarizing source texts. A thesis located anywhere in the essay may earn the point (including a concluding thesis); the thesis is evaluated entirely independently from the successful development of the argument and may earn the point even if the rest of the response does not support the same line of reasoning. The thesis does not need to be a single sentence, but separate sentences must be in close proximity. For AP Literature the thesis must “present an interpretation.” The rubric removed language requiring the thesis to "establish a line of reasoning."

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Commentary (4 points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must provide evidence for their position and expand on it with commentary that connects the evidence to their position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category is weighted most heavily (4 of 6 points). The source/type of evidence varies by essay type (e.g., synthesis vs. rhetorical analysis vs. literary analysis). Decision rules describe "typical" responses for each score level; determining what meets the level of "explanation" is often the hardest judgment. If a student has provided explanation but not very successfully, they may still earn a mid-level score (e.g., a 3). If on the fence, favor rewarding students for what they do well. Note: an essay that does NOT earn the Thesis point is highly unlikely to earn 3 or 4 points in Evidence and Commentary. Also: grammatical/mechanical errors are generally not the focus, but if errors are so frequent/significant that they interfere with understanding, the student is ineligible for the fourth point in this reporting category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication (1 point)
rubrics_metrics.description: The response must "demonstrate sophistication of thought and/or a complex understanding of the rhetorical situation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophistication must be integrated into the argument (not a passing phrase or reference). The scoring notes list 3–4 ways students might demonstrate sophistication, but the criterion is rigorous and should not be treated as a simple checklist. Examples of authentic sophistication include relevant analogies, discussion of alternative interpretations, or other complex engagements with the text; the rubric removed earlier language that suggested merely appropriate prose style would suffice. Teachers should encourage creative, substantive engagement rather than box-checking strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rules (essay-type-specific scoring guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: College Board decision rules accompany the analytic rubrics and vary by essay type, providing more specific application guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision rules include descriptions of "typical" responses at each score level and clarifications that help scorers apply the criteria. They differ across prompts (AP Language Q1/Q2/Q3; AP Literature Q1/Q2/Q3) and clarify subtle points (e.g., thesis location, what counts as adequate explanation, evidence sourcing). Readers should consult the complete revised rubrics with decision rules for each question type when scoring. Use these rules to resolve close calls and to align classroom instruction to scoring expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic rubric weighting (1/4/1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays are evaluated out of 6 possible points across three scoring categories: Thesis (1), Evidence and Commentary (4), Sophistication (1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because four of six points are in Evidence and Commentary, instruction and scoring should prioritize students' use of evidence and development of commentary. The distribution means overall scores can reflect different strengths across categories (two essays with the same total score might have very different category profiles), so avoid equating overall score with a single holistic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common scoring mistakes / anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent errors scorers make that misapply the rubric or over-weight irrelevant features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't focus on grammar and mechanics (they're relatively unimportant unless errors block understanding, per Evidence & Commentary rules). Don't penalize students for missing conclusions—conclusions are not required. Don't be fooled by flowery or sophisticated surface prose if the essay fails to analyze evidence or support the argument—sound style does not substitute for development and analysis. Avoid comparing the new analytic scores to the old 0–9 holistic scores; the analytic rubric requires a different mindset and direct category-based calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching implications and student-facing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How teachers should use the rubric to guide instruction and what to teach students to meet rubric expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to rely upon the text, distinguish summary from analysis, and elaborate upon analysis. Emphasize planning before writing so students know their thesis and can keep the piece focused. Teach how to write a clear, defensible thesis (and practice placing/underlining it for scorer visibility). Give repeated practice with evidence-selection and commentary strategies. Encourage creative engagement (e.g., analogies, alternative interpretations) to develop real sophistication, but discourage teaching empty "check-the-box" tactics. Use rubric language for self-assessment and peer review in class.
